tagline: Salt lakes and ships at Africa's gateway
overview:
Djibouti is a small, sun-baked country on the Horn of Africa, guarding the narrow strait where the Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden. It is about the size of New Jersey, wedged between Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia, with Yemen just across the water. Its location is its treasure: nearly all ships sailing between Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal pass by, and Djibouti's port also handles almost all the trade of its giant landlocked neighbor, Ethiopia.

About one million people live in Djibouti, and around two-thirds of them are in the capital, Djibouti City, which has the same name as the country. Arabic and French are official languages, and Somali and Afar are the languages of the two main peoples. Nearly everyone is Muslim. The country is a republic led by a president, and its stability in a troubled region has led France, the United States, China, Japan, and other nations to keep military bases there. The land is mostly desert, so most food is imported, and camels still cross the plains.
landAndNature: Djibouti sits where three pieces of the Earth's crust are pulling apart, and the results are dramatic. Lake Assal, a salt lake 155 meters below sea level, is the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth, ringed by a blinding white crust that people have mined for centuries. Lake Abbe, on the Ethiopian border, has a field of limestone chimneys up to 50 meters tall that steam in the dawn light. Volcanic plains of black rock stretch between them. The Goda Mountains in the north hold the small Day Forest, a surprising patch of juniper trees. The Gulf of Tadjoura draws whale sharks every winter, and the coral reefs are rich in fish. It is one of the hottest countries in the world, with summer highs above 45 degrees Celsius.
peopleAndCulture: The Somali, mainly of the Issa clan, and the Afar are the two main peoples, and both have traditions of nomadic herding, poetry, and long negotiations under acacia trees. Daily life includes chewing khat leaves in the afternoon, sipping spiced tea, and eating skoudehkaris, a rice dish with lamb and spices, or lahoh, spongy flatbread, often with French baguettes on the side. Women wear bright, flowing dresses; men often wear a wrapped skirt called a macawiis. Music is drum-based and lively, and traditional dances tell stories of clans and camels. Soccer is popular, and Djiboutian runners have competed in the Olympic marathon. Fishing dhows share the harbor with container ships and warships.
history: Afar and Somali herders have moved across this land for centuries, trading with Arabia and Ethiopia through small ports like Tadjoura and Zeila. France gained a foothold in 1862 and created the colony of French Somaliland, building Djibouti City and, in 1917, a railway to Addis Ababa that made it Ethiopia's link to the sea. In votes in 1958 and 1967 the territory chose to stay French, but independence finally came on June 27, 1977. Hassan Gouled Aptidon was the first president, ruling until 1999, when his nephew Ismaïl Omar Guelleh succeeded him. A civil war between the government and Afar rebels lasted from 1991 to 1994 and ended in a peace deal. A new electric railway to Ethiopia opened in 2018.
funFacts: Lake Assal is about ten times saltier than the ocean and lies 155 meters below sea level, the lowest point in Africa.
Djibouti hosts military bases from more foreign countries than any other nation, including the United States, France, China, and Japan.
The country's economy depends so heavily on its port that it handles roughly 95 percent of Ethiopia's foreign trade.
The limestone chimneys of Lake Abbe were used as an alien landscape in the 1968 film Planet of the Apes.
Whale sharks, the largest fish in the world, gather in the Gulf of Tadjoura each winter and can be snorkeled alongside.
